title: Unless a grain of wheat falls (John 12:12–26)
hook: a seed must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary poured nard on Jesus's feet in Bethany, and the house was filled with the scent. Your line was the house was filled. What extravagant thing did you do? Day six hundred twenty-six.

The next day, the city is packed for Passover, and word spreads that Jesus is coming. A great crowd goes out to meet him. John tells us what they carried: "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna is a Hebrew cry, save us, now. Jesus finds a young donkey and rides in on it. The religious leaders watch the crowds and say to one another: "behold, the world is gone after him." And then, as if to prove them right, some Greeks arrive.

These Greeks are pilgrims, outsiders who have come up to worship at the feast. They go to Philip and ask politely: "Sir, we would see Jesus." Philip tells Andrew, and together they tell Jesus. You'd expect him to say, bring them in. Instead, he says the hour has come. And then he talks about a seed. "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Corn, in the King James Bible, means any grain: here, a single grain of wheat. Kept in a jar, it stays a grain forever. Safe, whole, and alone. Planted, buried in the dark, it breaks open and stops being a seed. And then it becomes a stalk heavy with grain. Jesus is talking about his own death. The Greeks want to see him, and his answer is: the way the world will see me is through my dying. One grain becomes a harvest. Then he widens it to everyone who follows him: "He that loveth his life shall lose it." Not a call to despise life, but to let go of clutching it. The verse has traveled. Dostoevsky put it at the front of The Brothers Karamazov, as the epigraph for the whole book. Farmers know it without any book: you can't eat your seed grain and have a harvest too. Christians often read these words at funerals, and whenever something has to end so something else can begin.
screen: `A GRAIN IN A JAR STAYS ALONE.`
then, large: `EXCEPT A CORN OF WHEAT FALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing go. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been holding onto too tightly. An old plan that isn't working. A grudge. A version of yourself you've outgrown. A role, a possession, a need to be right. Hold it like a seed in your palm. Notice how hard you're gripping. Then imagine opening your hand and letting it fall into the ground. You don't have to know what will grow from it. If you pray, you can place it in God's hands. If you don't, simply notice what your open hand feels like. The bell holds the time.
Grain. A single seed of wheat, Jesus says, that must fall into the ground and die before it can bear much fruit.
Your line: unless it dies. Today, let one small thing go on purpose, and leave room for what might grow. Day six hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Christians remember the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, often carrying palms; the grain of wheat saying is often read at funerals and in Holy Week.

original.note: Greek: a grain, a seed. A single grain of wheat in John 12:24.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saying about gardening, or about sacrifice in general.
what it means: when outsiders ask to see him, Jesus speaks of his death as a seed that must be buried to become a harvest.
what a scholar hears: the Greeks' arrival marks "the hour" in John, the turn from signs to glory; Dostoevsky made this verse the epigraph of The Brothers Karamazov.

notes: Hosanna from Hebrew hoshi'a na, 'save, please/now' (Psalm 118:25). Confirm.
'Only John tells us what they carried': palms specified only in John (Matthew/Mark: branches; Luke: none). Confirm.
The Greeks (Hellenes) are often read as Gentile God-fearers; the script says 'outsiders'. Confirm.
Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880) carries John 12:24 as epigraph. Confirm.
Philip's Greek name and Bethsaida origin (12:21); confirm 'has a Greek name'.
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the 'only John' superlative (voice and myth), 'who has a Greek name', 'dozens of grains', 'his last novel', and the unsourced Easter reading.
